issues.note: Common idiom; few is the first content word, so it is keyed here.
The few/a few contrast is repeated across core idea, explanations, note.
Quite a few means a fairly large number, so it contradicts sense 2.
The forms are fewer and fewest; the example phrases show learner errors.
Quite a few is idiomatic and needs its own phrase and definition.
Few means not many and goes before plural countable nouns.
A few cannot go with uncountable money; the example is ungrammatical.
Restates the learner-error and compare notes on little.
Ungrammatical example that contradicts the entry's own learner error.
Correctly flags both contradictions with the rest of the entry.
Second clause repeats the first; the contrast is stated elsewhere already.

findings.F1: The idiom few and far between is missing from phrases.
findings.F2: The few versus a few contrast is stated redundantly in many fields.
findings.F3: Quite a few (a fairly large number) is listed as a collocation of 'a small number' instead of being its own phrase.
findings.F4: The usage note gives the comparative and superlative as less and least instead of fewer and fewest.
findings.F5: Sense 1 is defined for uncountable nouns and 'not much' instead of plural nouns and 'not many'.
findings.F6: Sense 2 example 'Could I borrow a few money?' is ungrammatical.
findings.F7: The adaptation grammar note restates the countability fact already given in the learner errors and the compare note.

missed: The inflections table is empty although few has the comparative fewer and the superlative fewest; it needs gradability codes so that these forms are generated.
